Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Elena remembered the house on Elm Street through the cold draft of kitchen tiles against her small knees. Her stepfather's temper had been a sudden, physical force, swinging in the narrow hallways when she failed to keep the noise down. He had grabbed her wrists, his hands bruising her skin, and shoved her into the corner until she lay still. The violence was absolute in the moment, but over the decades, it had slipped into a strange, flat distance. When she tried to recount the years of that house, the words felt detached, as if she were reading about someone else's childhood. Yet, without warning, a sharp fragment would surface-the specific smell of his tobacco mixed with the sting of a fall onto hardwood-before vanishing again. She often found herself doubting the reality of it, wondering if the sheer brutality of those memories meant they were just a story her mind had invented. That doubt and the sudden, unbidden fragments began to color how she moved through the world. When a memory piece surfaced during a quiet shift, the clinical air of the rehabilitation center seemed to thin. The raw intensity of the images would convince her that the danger was no longer in the past, and that threat from strangers was imminent. It did not matter that she was surrounded by colleagues; a man in a delivery uniform or a neighbor walking his dog could make her pulse jump with the same old terror. The feeling that she was constantly being watched would settle in her chest, tightening until she needed her back against the wall. She would drag her treatment chair into the corner of the exam room, placing her spine firmly against the plaster so she could watch the entire space, and she would wake during the night to check whether she was safe, crawling to the edge of her bed whenever a floorboard creaked. The constant sense that strangers approached with malice, paired with the exhaustion of waking alert throughout the night, left her with little energy to cope. That rising alarm would then spill directly into her evening routines. She began to avoid anything that could be stressful, declining invitations and refusing overtime, because she believed any new demand might spark the same panic. When avoidance failed, she would retreat to the kitchen and clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control. The ritual offered temporary stability, but when the stress returned, she would open the pantry and overeat, eating excessively to manage distress and push back against the numb recall that always followed the panic. Her hyper-vigilance in the clinic, constantly scanning for the threat of strangers and needing her back against the wall, did more than protect her; it kept her nervous system primed. This heightened state of alarm would then pull the traumatic memories forward, making the story feel unreal one moment and terrifyingly present the next. The flat, detached way she could recount the abuse, combined with these unbidden flashes, made her feel fundamentally unmoored, which is why she began to avoid anything that could be stressful, turning instead to cleaning and overeating to manage the distress. By systematically avoiding stressors and filling her time with these routines, she had built a fragile buffer against the past. But when she finally stopped to rest, that very avoidance meant the memories returned unfiltered, surfacing as sudden pieces that felt impossible to dismiss. After her divorce, she had moved to a quieter apartment, but the isolation only deepened the loop. She had managed her work for years by meticulously organizing every therapy mat and ball, but recently, the routine had broken. She found herself weeping in her car after a long day, overwhelmed by the realization that she was fifty-nine, yet still moving through her clinic as if expecting the next blow. It was the way she had started flinching at a resident's light touch during a gait assessment, coupled with the sudden, unbidden memory of her stepfather's grip that had finally pushed her to seek therapy. She came to the appointment hoping to finally break the cycle, terrified that the memories might consume her, but desperately wanting to stop living in the shadow of a house that no longer existed.
